summary: Space Simulator – Build Your Rocket is a pixel-art educational game where players design, fund, launch and operate a small spacecraft. Inside their own space station, players choose a mission (the Moon first, then Mars), buy parts in a shop and assemble a CubeSat-inspired ship in the hangar. Every choice (launcher, motor, solar panels, antenna, science instrument, radiation shielding) changes weight, energy, cost and score. If the pre-flight check is red and the player launches anyway, the rocket fails during ascent and funds are lost. On success, players land on the Moon to repair a lunar relay, or on Mars to deploy a drone, inspired by NASA's Ingenuity helicopter, that explores and returns. A final science report shows what the instrument discovered and how each decision shaped the result. A "What if...?" panel lets players test part changes before committing. The game teaches that space missions are about trade-offs: budget, mass, power, data and risk.
details:
WHAT IT DOES: The player builds and flies space missions. In the station, the player picks a mission, buys parts, equips the ship and checks the flight list. The launch animation, the trip, and the landing on the Moon or Mars follow. On the Moon the player collects parts and repairs a relay robot; on Mars the player deploys a drone that explores and returns. At the end, a science report shows data collected, a discovery, the consequences of each decision and a score.

HOW IT WORKS: Each part has mass, power use, cost and capability. The game checks mass limits, power balance, data link, radiation shielding, motor capability and launcher reach. If checks fail and the player launches anyway, the rocket is damaged during ascent and funds are lost. A "What if...?" panel simulates replacing any part without changing the real ship.

IMPACT: It lets students experience systems engineering: budget, mass, power, communications and risk. Players learn why every choice has a trade-off.

REAL-WORLD INSPIRATION: ship sizes follow CubeSat standards (1U, 3U, 6U); the drone is inspired by NASA's Ingenuity Mars Helicopter; the launch-safety pins follow typical CubeSat requirements; destinations include LEO, polar, geostationary, lunar and Mars orbits. Numeric values (costs, watts, data rates, science points) are simplified for gameplay and are not mission data.

TOOLS: Python, pygame, OpenCV (menu video), PyInstaller (Windows executable), Git and GitHub, Canva.

CREATIVITY: pixel-art style, walkable space station, animated launch with failure sequence, drone expedition with progress bar, and a final cinematic.

AI USE: parts of the code and text were developed with AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic), reviewed and tested by the team.
